answer: Model the 1950s alteration as an E81 Transformation, not an E11 Modification / P31 has modified. The bodice was unpicked, the silk and lace panels recut and restitched, and the worn skirt fabric discarded outright -- the original wedding gown (E22 Human-Made Object) does not survive intact as the same unit of documentation; a new, distinct object (the christening gown, E22) comes into existence that preserves recognizable substance (the silk/lace) but has a fundamentally different nature and identity (different garment, different structure, part of the original matter discarded rather than retained). The E11 declaration itself carves this out of its own scope: 'An event should also be documented using an instance of E81 Transformation if it results in the destruction of one or more objects and the simultaneous production of others using parts or material from the originals. In this case, the new items have separate identities.' Use P124 transformed (E81 -> the wedding gown, taken out of existence) and P123 resulted in (E81 -> the christening gown, brought into existence). Two SIG decisions confirm this reading: Issue 12, which created the Transformation class in the first place, gives 'a piece of money becoming a piece of jewelry' as its own worked example of an object that 'preserves some recognizable identity' while becoming a new thing -- structurally identical to fabric from one garment becoming another garment. And Issue 287 records the SIG choosing E81 over E11 for a materially analogous case (print matrices) precisely because 'the matrix has a distinct identity both before and after the change... [even though] there can be considerable physical change to the plate.'

rejected_alternatives.why_not: E11's own scope note excludes this case: 'An event should also be documented using an instance of E81 Transformation if it results in the destruction of one or more objects and the simultaneous production of others using parts or material from the originals. In this case, the new items have separate identities.' E11 is for changes that leave one object's identity intact; here the wedding gown as a unit of documentation ends (skirt fabric discarded, bodice unpicked) and a different garment begins.

E81's declaration distinguishes itself from 're-classifications (documented using E17 Type Assignment)... of objects that do not fundamentally change their nature or identity.' The change here is not a re-typing of one persisting physical unit -- material was physically cut, recombined, and partly discarded -- so E17 alone would understate what happened.
